page.title: Files as a database
page.kicker: Lecture 10 · week 5, day 2 · running case: a word dictionary with no database, then Bitcask
page.dek: Two storage engines built from plain files: a read-only dictionary on S3 with a header, an index and a weekly merge, and an append-only key-value store with one map in memory, revealed at the end as Bitcask.
page.description: Lecture 10: build a portable word dictionary with no database, served from one file on S3 by pointed reads and updated weekly, then design an append-only key-value store on cheap disks and meet Bitcask.

chapters.title: A dictionary with no database
chapters.summary: Serve every English word and its meaning with no database at all: one portable file, read-mostly, updated every Sunday. First the requirements, then the format, then the clever ideas set aside.

chapters.title: Finding one word fast
chapters.summary: The naive lookup reads half a terabyte per request. One small index, and one multiplication, turn it into a single pointed read.

chapters.title: One file you can ship
chapters.summary: The index made two files, and the brief said one. Putting both in one file raises a new question: where does the index stop? The answer is the header, the trick behind every file format.

chapters.title: Serving it from S3
chapters.summary: One file, many API servers. Copying it to each server is the obvious move and the costly one. Pin down the property you need, random reads over the network, and S3 turns the file into a database.

chapters.title: The weekly update
chapters.summary: Sunday's changelog changes apple's meaning. You can't edit a file in place, so build a new one, and keeping the file sorted makes that a single merge pass.

chapters.title: Switching every server to the new file
chapters.summary: The new dictionary is ready. Overwrite the old one and servers read garbage. Upload it to a new path, point a small meta.json at it, and let a routine deployment do the reload. Then see why reading a few bytes from S3 matters so much.

chapters.title: Fast writes on a cheap disk
chapters.summary: The second engine must take writes as fast as a magnetic disk allows, and lose nothing. Append every put to the end of one file, make delete a put, and keep one map in memory for reads.

chapters.title: Files that never stop growing
chapters.summary: The store never deletes anything from disk, so it fills up. Split it into small files with one active writer, merge and compact the old ones, and watch disk usage draw a sawtooth.

chapters.title: Record format and integrity
chapters.summary: "Write key, value" is too casual. Prefix every record with its sizes so one read gets it all, and lead with a CRC so a half-written record is caught, not served.

chapters.title: It's called Bitcask
chapters.summary: One map of keys in memory, append-only files on disk, merges in the background, a CRC on every record: that is Bitcask. What it can't do, where it runs, and how it differs from the LSM trees coming next week.

chapters.title: What to keep
chapters.summary: The same few ideas built both engines. Here they are side by side, with the heuristics the class kept returning to, and where the course goes next.
